title: Softr Alternatives: How to Pick the Right Platform for Portals and Business Apps
summary: Softr alternatives compared: Jet Admin, Noloco, Stacker, Glide, Bubble, WeWeb, FlutterFlow and AppSheet on data sources, permissions and pricing.
body_markdown:
Softr made client portals approachable. Point it at Airtable, pick a block, publish. The trouble starts when the portal succeeds: the flow needs a second drill-down, the data outgrows a spreadsheet, someone asks who can see which rows, and the plan that unlocks any of it costs several times the one you are on.


This guide covers the nine credible replacements, says plainly which fits which situation, and ends with a migration checklist. Every price below was rechecked against the vendor's own pricing page on September 26, 2026, with the billing toggle switched to monthly — several of these pages default to the discounted annual rate.


> For governed portals and internal tools on the database you already run, Jet Admin. For an Airtable-native portal that looks like Softr but goes further, Noloco. For portals with large external audiences and no per-seat charges, Stacker. For spreadsheet-backed apps with almost no learning curve, Glide. For a full SaaS product, Bubble. For a front end on your own backend, WeWeb. For genuinely native mobile, FlutterFlow or Adalo. And if your company runs on Google Workspace, AppSheet.

## What is Softr, and why look for alternatives?


Softr builds client portals and simple internal apps from pre-made blocks on top of Airtable, Google Sheets or a database. No canvas, no components to wire: you pick a list block, point it at a table, and publish. That constraint is the product, and it is why non-technical teams ship something in an afternoon. Teams leave for four reasons.


### The flow needs more than one drill-down


There is no traditional drag-and-drop builder, so you cannot reach individual inputs, actions and variables. Take a realistic support flow: select a customer, view their transactions, open one, check its log, issue a refund. That is one screen sequence with three levels of related data, and Softr is not designed for it. This is the limitation that sends the most teams looking.


### The data outgrows a spreadsheet


Softr does not connect to MongoDB, Firebase, Snowflake or GraphQL. That is irrelevant for an early project and decisive for one built on a real backend. Airtable itself caps standard plans at 50,000 records per base, so the ceiling often arrives from the data side before the builder side.


### Permissions stop short of what a real portal needs


Once external customers log in, the questions become specific: is access enforced per row rather than per page, is there an audit trail, and does sign-on go through the identity provider the company already uses. Real access control and SSO arrive only on higher tiers.


### The plan that unlocks it costs nearly five times as much


This is the reason people phrase most bluntly. Custom code and API connectors are not on the entry plan. Getting them means the Pro tier at $119 a month, against $25 for Basic, and the free plan stops at 5 app users and 5,000 database records. Teams discover this after the portal is built, which is the worst moment to discover it. Softr pricing checked September 26, 2026.


### When Softr is still the right choice


If the data fits comfortably in Airtable, the portal is a read-mostly view with simple forms, and nobody is asking for row-level rules or an audit log, Softr does this faster than anything else here. Switching would cost you a fortnight and buy nothing.


## Types of Softr alternatives


The alternatives to Softr fall into five categories, and deciding which one you need removes most of the list before you compare a single feature.


- Portal builders on a spreadsheet-style backend. The nearest thing to a like-for-like swap. Noloco, Stacker, Glide.
- Governed app platforms on your own data. The portal plus the permissions, workflows and deployment options a security review asks about. Jet Admin.
- Full app platforms. You are no longer building a portal, you are building a product. Bubble, WeWeb.
- Native mobile builders. When the deliverable is genuinely an app in a store. FlutterFlow, Adalo.
- Ecosystem-bundled options. Sensible when the company already pays for the suite. AppSheet.


## What to look for


Six dimensions settle most of these evaluations. Data connectivity, meaning whether the platform reaches the database you actually run rather than a copy of it. Flow depth, meaning how many levels of related data one screen sequence can handle before you are stuck. Permissions, and specifically whether they reach the row and the field or stop at the page. External user pricing, because a portal is a tool whose cost grows with its success, and per-customer tiers behave very differently from flat plans. Deployment, since self-hosting is either mandatory for you or irrelevant and that one answer removes half the list. And what happens on the plan above the one you are quoting, because that is where the features you will need in six months usually live.


## 1. Jet Admin, best for governed portals on the data you already run


**Pros and cons.** Covers the same portals and internal tools as Softr but connects straight to your production database, with permissions and workflows included rather than tiered. It is not the tool for public marketing sites or consumer web apps, and if your data genuinely lives in Airtable and always will, a portal builder is less machinery.


**Key features.** Connects your own databases, APIs and warehouses rather than a copy, with blending across sources in one table. Granular access to UI components: individual input fields placed anywhere on the canvas, values passed from a clicked table row into another page to filter or pre-fill it. Server-side dynamic filtering for multi-tenancy, approval flows, JSON transforms and complex conditionals without code, with JavaScript available almost anywhere to extend it. Figma import alongside the drag-and-drop builder. Row-level permissions, SSO (Business and above) and self-hosted, on-premise or air-gapped deployment (Enterprise).


**Pricing.** Free $0, Pro $20 a month ($16 billed annually), Business $100 ($80 annually), Enterprise custom. Every plan includes unlimited apps, unlimited users and unlimited workflows; what changes between tiers is the monthly AI credit allowance and the collaboration, security and support features. Credits are consumed when the AI builder generates an app, not when people use one — so a portal's user count does not drive the bill. Customer Portal plans follow the same structure. Checked September 26, 2026.


**Best for** teams whose Softr portal has become a business system: real customer logins, rules about who sees which records, and data that was never going to stay in a spreadsheet. Founded in 2018 with pre-seed backing from Y Combinator, bootstrapped since, based in San Francisco.


## 2. Noloco, best for an Airtable-native portal that goes further


**Pros and cons.** The closest thing to Softr in spirit, with more depth on records, roles and workflows. Same conceptual ceiling, since it is still built around the Airtable-style model. Unlike Softr it does not meter builder seats separately at the entry tier — team seats are pooled — though records and active clients are both capped.


**Key features.** Client and team portals on Airtable, HubSpot or a database, with granular field and record permissions, workflow automation and a hosted no-code canvas.


**Pricing.** A free plan exists: $0 with unlimited team seats, 50 active clients and 2,000 records. Build is $79 a month, or $65 billed annually, with 10 team seats (additional at $6 each), 1,000 active clients and 25,000 records (additional 25,000 at $25). Enterprise is a custom quote. A 14-day full-feature trial needs no card. Checked September 26, 2026.


**Best for** teams who like the Softr approach and simply need more control over what each customer sees.


## 3. Stacker, best for credit-priced portals and AI agents


**Pros and cons.** Now trading as stacker.ai, and repositioned since many comparisons were written: it has moved from per-customer portal pricing to AI agents billed by credits. The upside is that there are no per-seat charges at all, so a portal with many external users no longer steps up in price. The downside is the usual one with credit models - consumption is harder to forecast than a seat count.


**Key features.** Portals on Airtable and Salesforce data, per-user and per-record permissions, and a mature portal-specific feature set rather than a general app builder.


**Pricing.** From $50 a month for 250 credits, scaling to $2,000 for 10,000 credits at a flat $0.20 per credit. No per-seat charges, and $100 of non-expiring trial credits to start. Checked September 26, 2026.


**Best for** client portals with large or growing external audiences, where per-seat pricing elsewhere would be the binding cost - provided you can estimate credit consumption.


## 4. Glide, best for spreadsheet-backed apps with almost no learning curve


**Pros and cons.** The fastest route from a spreadsheet to something that looks like an app, and strong on mobile. Business logic beyond the straightforward gets awkward. Note that Glide now presents itself as GlideOS and meters credits rather than the older Individual/Maker/Business seat tiers — comparisons written against those tier names are describing a model it no longer sells.


**Key features.** Apps on Google Sheets, Glide Tables or a connected database, mobile-first layouts, AI features and a large template library.


**Pricing.** Free $0 with limited credits, 2 team members, 10 projects and — importantly — zero published apps and zero enabled workflows. Basic $25 a month (100 credits, 2 published apps, 1 workflow), Plus $50 (250 credits, 3 members, 5 published apps), Pro $125 (500 credits plus 50 per additional member, unlimited published apps and workflows), Enterprise custom. Checked September 26, 2026.


**Worth checking yourself.** Because the product repositioned, review-site scores and roundups may describe the earlier Glide rather than GlideOS. Read the dates before weighting them.


**Best for** internal or field apps where the data already lives in a sheet and the job is to make it usable on a phone.


## 5. Bubble, best when you are building a product, not a portal


**Pros and cons.** The most customisable option here by a distance, and the only one that genuinely targets public-facing SaaS. In exchange your app lives in Bubble’s runtime and database, and the learning curve is weeks rather than hours.


**Key features.** Full visual development with its own database, workflow engine and plugin marketplace, plus a large third-party template ecosystem.


**Pricing.** Free $0 for development with 50,000 workload units a month. Starter $69 a month ($59 billed annually) with 175,000 units, Growth $249 ($209) with 250,000, Team $649 ($549) with 500,000, Enterprise custom. The page defaults to annual billing, so the first figure you see is the discounted one. Checked September 26, 2026.


**Best for** teams whose Softr portal was actually the first version of a product.


## 6. WeWeb, best for a front end on a backend you control


**Pros and cons.** Gives you the interface layer and leaves the backend to you, which is exactly right if you already have one and wrong if you do not. Code export keeps vendor risk low.


**Key features.** Visual front-end builder over any REST API, Supabase, Xano or SQL, with code export and self-hosting options.


**Pricing.** Two stacked bills. The builder: Free $0 (1 million AI tokens), Essential $20 a month (10 million tokens, code export, GitHub sync), Pro from roughly $50 up to $300 depending on the token tier. Hosting is priced separately as WeWeb Cloud — Free, Launch+ $13, Grow+ $20, Scale+ $66, Power $208. Budget both lines, not just the builder. Annual billing saves up to 20%. Checked September 26, 2026.


**Best for** teams with an existing backend and developers who want to stop hand-building admin screens.


## 7. FlutterFlow, best for genuinely native mobile apps


**Pros and cons.** Produces real Flutter applications for iOS and Android, which none of the portal builders do. Closer to development than to no-code, so expect to think about state and data models.


**Key features.** Visual Flutter builder with Firebase and Supabase integration, custom code injection and full source export to the app stores.


**Pricing.** Free $0 with up to 2 projects and 10 Lite credits. Basic $39 a month adds unlimited projects, code and APK download and custom-domain web publishing. Growth is $80 for the first seat and $55 for the second; Business $150 for the first seat and $85 for seats two to five. Annual billing saves roughly 25%. Checked September 26, 2026.


**Best for** teams whose requirement is an app in the store rather than a responsive web portal.


## 8. Adalo, best for simple consumer-style mobile apps


**Pros and cons.** The gentlest path to a mobile app in this list, with a component model non-technical users pick up quickly. It struggles once the data volume or the logic grows.


**Key features.** Drag-and-drop mobile and web app builder with its own collections, external API connections and app store publishing.


**Pricing.** Free $0 publishes nothing — 500 records per app, 1 editor, unlimited test apps. Starter $45 a month ($36 billed annually) for 1 published app, Professional $65 ($52) for 2 published apps and 5 editors, Team $200 ($160) for 5 apps and 10 editors. Adalo advertises no usage-based charges on top. Checked September 26, 2026.


**Best for** straightforward member or booking style apps where polish matters more than depth.


## 9. AppSheet, best inside Google Workspace


**Pros and cons.** Cheap per user and deeply tied into Google, which decides it for a lot of organisations before any feature comparison happens. The interface feels dated next to everything else here.


**Key features.** Apps generated from Google Sheets, Cloud SQL or Excel, with offline support, automation and Workspace admin controls.


**Pricing.** You can build and test with up to 10 users at no cost. Starter $5 per user a month, Core $10 (and included in most paid Google Workspace plans), Enterprise Plus $20. Checked September 26, 2026.


**Best for** business units already standardised on Google Workspace building operational apps on sheets they own.


## Also worth knowing


Plasmic is a visual builder aimed at teams who want to hand off to React rather than stay in a canvas. Tadabase and Zite both publish credible comparisons in this space and are themselves portal-capable builders. For teams staying inside Airtable, Pory, MiniExtensions and CollabPortals extend it directly rather than replacing it, which is often cheaper than a migration if the only problem is one missing view.


## Why the data source decides more than the builder


Most comparisons of these tools argue about blocks and canvases. In practice the thing that determines whether the app survives its second year is what it reads from.


A portal on a spreadsheet inherits the spreadsheet’s ceilings: the record cap, the absence of real types and relations, the fact that permissions belong to the file rather than to the row. Airtable’s 50,000 records per base on standard plans is the version of this ceiling most teams meet first. Nothing in the builder layer fixes it, and every migration away from it costs more the longer the portal has been live.


So the useful question at the start is not which builder is nicest, but where this data will live in two years. If the answer is a real database, choose a tool that can read one now rather than a tool you will replace when it does.


## How to Evaluate Softr Alternatives in 20–30 Minutes


Rather than reading feature lists for weeks, build a small test app that mirrors your real needs. Here's a rapid evaluation playbook:


**Your test scenario** : A client portal where internal staff upload documents and external users log in, see only their company's records, submit requests, and track status.


**Steps to follow in each candidate tool** :


1. Connect one real data source (your Airtable base, a PostgreSQL database, or a Google Sheet)
2. Create two roles: staff (internal) and client (external)
3. Implement record-level permissions so each client sees only their own data
4. Add a 3-step workflow: submit → review → approve
5. Build a basic reporting dashboard showing request status counts


Run this exercise in 2–3 shortlisted tools. For example, try Softr, Jet Admin, and one Airtable-centric tool like Noloco. Time each build and note friction points.


**What to watch for** :


- How clear and granular are the permissions settings?
- Does connecting your data source require workarounds or transformations?
- Do external users count toward billing limits, and how?
- How much configuration is needed for even simple automations?
- Can you theme and brand the portal with a custom domain?


This exercise will reveal more about fit than any feature comparison table.


## Selection Guide: Best Softr Alternative by Team Type and Skills


The same platform won't suit everyone. Choosing a platform often depends on whether you're building a public website or private portal, and decisions should reflect who will build and maintain apps.


- **Non-technical operations teams** building internal dashboards and simple client portals: Start with Noloco or Stacker if you're on Airtable. Both offer intuitive drag and drop interfaces and handle role-based access without code.
- **Mixed ops + IT teams** with some SQL/API knowledge needing governed internal tools: Jet Admin fits well here. It connects to your own database and existing data, supports complex permissions, and lets IT manage governance while ops owns the day-to-day configuration.
- **Product or engineering teams** comfortable with code: Bubble or WeWeb for custom web apps; FlutterFlow for native mobile app development. These are full app builder platforms where a steeper learning curve pays off in customization. Retool is powerful for building and managing internal tools if you're engineering-led and need quick internal apps.
- **Agencies needing repeatable branded portals** : CollabPortals or Pory for Airtable-only portals with unlimited users; Stacker for more polished external portals.
- **Customer-success teams** seeking self-service client portals: Prioritize external user pricing models and ease of branding. Jet Admin and Stacker both handle this well.
- **IT/infra teams** prioritizing SSO, SCIM, and audit trails: Jet Admin's governance stack is purpose-built for this, with SSO and audit logs on Business and SCIM on Enterprise. Some no-code platforms incorporate AI to aid in app generation, but governance depth matters more here.


For any system that stores or exposes customer data, involve ops, IT, and security in the evaluation together.


## Deployment, Governance, and Security Considerations


Deployment model and governance are often the deciding factors once organizations grow beyond early MVPs. A tool that works for a 20-user internal dashboard may fail compliance requirements when exposed to thousands of external clients in a regulated industry.


Most no code tools are SaaS-only, which is fine for many teams. But when data residency, network isolation, or on-premise integration matters, platforms like Jet Admin that support self-hosted or on-premise deployment (on its Enterprise plan) offer a meaningful advantage.


**Governance features to evaluate** :


- Role-based access control down to row, column, and action level
- SSO/SAML for enterprise identity management and SCIM for automated user provisioning
- Audit logs that track who did what, when
- Environment separation (dev/staging/prod) to prevent untested changes from reaching users interact with
- Approval workflows for schema or app changes


Softr typically sits at the lighter end of this spectrum: adequate for basic portals, but missing the depth required for handling PHI in healthcare, financial data under SOC 2, or large B2B client portals with strict contractual obligations.


Involve your security and compliance teams early. Request SOC 2 reports and data processing agreements from any vendor before committing production workloads.


## Migration Checklist: Moving from Softr to Another Platform


If you have an existing Softr app and you're planning a move, here's a practical checklist to reduce risk.


**1. Inventory your current setup** :


- List all apps and pages in your Softr workspace
- Identify underlying data sources (Airtable bases, Google Sheets, HubSpot, etc.)
- Document authentication flows, roles, and permission rules
- Catalog automations, integrations, webhooks, and any custom code or embeds


**2. Assess what can stay** : In many cases, your data can stay where it is. If your portal runs on Airtable, tools like Jet Admin, Noloco, and Stacker can connect directly to the same bases. This turns the migration into a UI and workflow rebuild rather than a data migration.


**3. Rebuild incrementally** :


- Pilot the migration with one critical workflow or one group of external users first
- Validate permissions, performance, and pricing assumptions before full cutover
- Re-implement any Softr-specific formulas or computed fields as logic in the new builder or as formulas in the data source


**4. Manage the transition** :


- Communicate changes to external users with clear timelines
- Train internal teams on the new platform
- Plan a phased cutover rather than a hard switch
- Monitor closely after launch for permission gaps, data sync issues, or performance regressions


**5. Model costs forward** : Because pricing varies (per-user, per-record, per-app, per-credit, flat), project costs for realistic growth in users and data. Zite offers unlimited users on every plan including free, at $25 a month for Pro ($20 billed annually) and $89 for Business ($75), while other platforms may charge per external user. Zite generates full apps from a single prompt, which can accelerate prototyping during evaluation.


## Conclusion: Which Softr Alternative Is Right for You?


The best softr alternative depends on your portal complexity, whether you're serving internal teams or external users (or both), your governance requirements, your data architecture, and your team's technical skills.


Simple rules of thumb: If you need a basic Airtable portal with simple roles, lightweight tools like Pory or CollabPortals may be enough. If you're building internal business tools or governed client portals with multiple data sources, role-based access, and compliance needs, Jet Admin is purpose-built for that scenario. If you need native mobile apps with app store publishing, FlutterFlow or Adalo are better fits. And if you're building a full SaaS product with complex logic, Bubble remains the deepest no code option.


Before committing, run the 20–30 minute evaluation exercise across your top two or three candidates. Build a real test with your own data, roles, and workflows. The friction you feel during that exercise will tell you more than any comparison article.


Ready to see how Jet Admin handles your use case?[Explore the customer portal page](https://www.jetadmin.io/customer-portal) to see how permissions, integrations, and branded portals work on your existing data, or browse the[integrations catalog](https://www.jetadmin.io/integrations) to confirm your data sources are supported.


## FAQ: Softr Alternatives and No-Code App Builders


### Can I keep my Airtable or Google Sheets data when moving away from Softr?


Yes. In most cases, your data layer (Airtable bases, Google Sheets, SQL databases) can remain unchanged while you switch the front-end from Softr to another platform. Many alternatives, including Jet Admin, Noloco, and Stacker, connect directly to the same data sources. This means migration is primarily a UI and workflow rebuild, not a data migration. Review any Softr-specific computed fields or formulas that may need to be reimplemented as logic in the new builder or within the data source itself.


### How do Softr alternatives charge for external users in client portals?


Pricing models vary significantly. Softr meters builders and app users separately, which can make large client portals expensive. Others offer flat fees with unlimited external users per portal (Pory, CollabPortals). Stacker and Glide now meter credits rather than seats, and Jet Admin includes unlimited users on every plan and meters AI credits for app generation instead. When evaluating, model your costs based on realistic user growth over the next 12–18 months rather than current headcount.


### What's the difference between AI code platforms and AI-powered app builders?


AI code platforms generate a codebase (e.g., React or Flutter) that your team must host, secure, and maintain like custom software. AI-powered app builders like Jet Admin apply AI to configure visual apps, automations, and data bindings on a managed no code platform without exposing raw code. Choose AI code generation when owning and extending the codebase is critical. Choose an ai powered app builder when speed, lower maintenance, and configurability for non-developers are higher priorities.


### Do I need developers to maintain a no-code portal or internal tool long term?


Many teams successfully operate these tools with operations or product managers as primary builders, especially for straightforward portals and internal dashboards. However, involving IT or developers becomes important as the app touches core systems, requires complex integrations, or must meet strict security requirements. A practical hybrid model works well: business users own day-to-day configuration while technical teams handle integrations, SSO, and governance.


### Should I prioritize app store publishing or web/PWA access for my use case?


Most client portals and internal business tools work well as responsive web apps or progressive web apps, which avoids app store submission and update overhead. Native mobile apps via FlutterFlow or Adalo are more appropriate when offline access, device hardware (camera, GPS via google maps), or consumer-style distribution through the apple app store is critical. Start with web/PWA unless you have a validated need for app store presence, and factor in total lifecycle costs and release management before committing to native builds.
